passages.text: In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each blank. The handloom has outlived every technology that was supposed to bury it. Each generation of mill owners has confidently announced its (1)______, and each has been obliged to watch the loom persist in villages where capital never quite arrived. Part of the explanation is economic: a loom costs little, occupies the corner of a house, and can be (2)______ by a family without wages, supervisors or shift timings. But economics alone cannot account for the stubbornness of the craft. A handwoven sari carries irregularities — a thickened weft here, a wandering border there — that a power loom is engineered to eliminate, and urban buyers have lately begun to (3)______ precisely those flaws as proof of human authorship. What the mill treats as defect, the market has learnt to read as signature. Policy, meanwhile, has been rather less helpful than its budgets would suggest. Schemes conceived in distant capitals tend to (4)______ weavers as beneficiaries rather than as entrepreneurs, dispensing subsidies while leaving the architecture of debt and middlemen wholly untouched. The weavers' own associations argue, with some justice, that what the trade needs is not charity but access — to yarn at fair prices, to contemporary design, and above all to the buyer, from whom they remain (5)______ by a chain of intermediaries who capture most of the margin.
